title: Nachiketa and the golden lid
word: reading the Isha in the original
hookLine: Death offers a boy gold and a long life to stop asking
carry: preya and shreya: the lovely can hide the good
tomorrow: what was a king thinking of when he died?

lines: KEEP THEM. I'LL TAKE THE ANSWER.
cards: A boy named Nachiketa ends up at the house of Yama, Death himself, and waits three nights at the door with no food. To make up for it, Yama grants him three wishes. The third: what happens to us after we die?
Yama flinches. Ask anything else, he says. Take sons and grandsons who live a hundred years.
As long a life as you like. Lovely companions, with chariots and music. Nachiketa says: those last till tomorrow.

teach.h: SHREYA: THE GOOD. PREYA: THE PLEASANT.
teach.b: This is the Katha Upanishad, and Yama's reply is one of Hinduism's great teachings. Two things come to every person, he says: shreya, the good, and preya, the pleasant. The wise one chooses the good.
You, Nachiketa, didn't take the golden chain so many sink in. Now Isha fifteen.

teach.h: BY A GOLDEN VESSEL, TRUTH'S FACE IS COVERED.
teach.b: Hiranmayena patrena satyasyapihitam mukham: by a golden vessel, the face of truth is covered. Not mud. Gold.
Something lovely in the way, like Yama's gifts. Then the request: tat tvam pushann apavrinu. Pushan, sun, uncover it, so I can see.
The next verse asks the sun to gather its rays, sees its loveliest form, and ends: so 'ham asmi. That one, I am. A neighbor tradition asks for a face too.

teach.h: NUMBERS: MAKE HIS FACE TO SHINE.
teach.b: In the priestly blessing in the Book of Numbers: The LORD make His face to shine upon thee, and be gracious unto thee. Jews still hear it as a blessing today.

teach.h: SO 'HAM ASMI: THAT ONE, I AM.
teach.b: What the two share: a longing for a bright face that doesn't stay hidden. An honest difference: the blessing keeps two, the LORD and the people.

The Isha's verse ends that one, I am, which Hindu schools read as oneness or as closest belonging. And the golden lid? Many Hindu teachers say it's mostly preya: the pleasant thing that's easy to stop at.

how: Isha 15 to 18 also appear in the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad, and some Hindus recite them near the end of life; the priestly blessing of Numbers 6 is said over congregations and children in Jewish life.

games.q: what does “reading the isha in the original” mean?
o: reading the Isha as a hymn praising gold
reading the Isha's rules for covering sacred things
reading the Isha's own words: a golden lid over truth's face

games.q: the boy, the lid, and a neighbor — tap the pairs.
p: make His face to shine upon thee

s: in the Katha, Nachiketa takes Yama's gold and long life
he says they last till tomorrow, and asks for the answer instead.
in the Isha, the face of truth is hidden by something lovely
a golden vessel: not mud, gold.
the Isha and the priestly blessing say exactly the same thing
both ask for a shining face; the blessing keeps God and people two, the Isha ends 'that one, I am.'

games.q: Yama offers Nachiketa gold, horses and a hundred-year life if he'll drop his question. by the Katha's teaching, what is the golden lid in that moment?
o: preya, the pleasant, standing in front of shreya, the good.
the question itself; Nachiketa should have taken the gifts.
gold as such; anything lovely is evil.
games.why: the gifts aren't evil; they're lovely, and that's the trouble. preya is easy to stop at. Nachiketa chose shreya, and the Isha asks the sun to lift the lid.

practice: Let your eyes rest on something softly bright nearby, a window or a lamp, never the sun. Notice the glow, then the thing the glow sits on: the frame, the shade. If you pray, ask the way the Isha asks: uncover it, so I can see.
Close your eyes and let the afterglow fade on its own.

wordCard.voice: Reading the Isha in the original, verses fifteen and sixteen: hiranmayena patrena, a golden lid over the face of truth, and a request to lift it.

orig.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: shreyas, the good, which Yama sets beside preyas, the pleasant, in the Katha Upanishad.

carryVoice: Your line: preya and shreya, the lovely can hide the good. Nachiketa saw through the gold. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Isha Upanishad 15 (hiranmayena patrena satyasyapihitam mukham; tat tvam pushann apavrinu satyadharmaya drishtaye)
Isha Upanishad 16 (pushann ekarshe yama surya ... yat te rupam kalyanatamam tat te pashyami ... so 'ham asmi)

Katha Upanishad 1.1.20–29 (Nachiketa's third wish; Yama's offers of long-lived sons, gold, horses, land, long life, companions with chariots and music; 'these last till tomorrow') and 1.2.1–3 (shreyas and preyas; the chain of wealth he did not take)
